headline: New moon springs load the narrows as bass and bunker collide at Stratford Shoal
subhead: Fluke slide out of the warming bays into the inlets while the Sound's middle stretch braces for its biggest tides since June.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it does in early July — it sat there and cooked. Light southwest wind most days, tides running on the smaller side coming off the last quarter, and the harbors and back bays climbing into the mid-to-upper 70s. That warmth is exactly why guys fishing Oyster Bay, Northport, and Port Jeff Harbor started seeing their fluke bite go soft on the inside — the same pattern that's been documented in the Great South Bay all week, where surface temps pushing near 79 degrees are shoving doormats out of the shallow bay water and into anything with current and a cooler bottom. In our zone that means the channels, the inlets, and the mouths of the harbors, not the flats where you found them in June.

This week changes the math. We're building toward a new moon on the 11th, and that means spring tides stacking up through the weekend — bigger swings, harder current, and a lot more water moving through the pinch points that make Central Sound what it is. Stratford Shoal and the Middle Ground Light rip are going to come alive with current the way they do every new and full moon, and that's when this stretch of water earns its name — the Sound narrows here, the tide has to squeeze through, and everything living in it gets funneled and stacked. The reopened PM flood-into-sunset window on the western end (right around the Kings Point high stand) is the first evening bite of real quality since the June full moon, and it's going to bleed east into our water as the tide timing shifts through the week. Peak alignment lands July 11-13 — that's your window.

On the water, the bass bite has been honest but not easy. Boats working the Stratford Shoal rip on the last of the outgoing have been picking at fish in the mid-20s to high-20s, mostly on bucktails — 1 to 1.5-ounce white or chartreuse, tipped with a strip of squid or a 4-inch white Gulp — bounced right through the rip structure in 25 to 40 feet where the current breaks over the shoal. It's not a wide-open bite. You need to hit the tide change right, and you need to be patient through a lot of nothing before the rod loads up. Middle Ground Light has been similar — better at first light and again in that last hour of daylight, live bunker on a fish-finder rig with 3 feet of 40-pound fluorocarbon leader has out-produced anything artificial when there's bait stacked, and there has been bait stacked. Bunker schools have been thick off Port Jeff and pushing west past Mount Sinai, and where you find the bunker balled up and nervous, the blues have been all over them — sometimes so aggressively you can see the surface boil from a quarter mile off. Bring wire or heavy mono leader if you're throwing metal into that — Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters have been getting bit fast and often once you find the school.

Fluke has been the more frustrating story. The inside-the-harbor bite has genuinely slowed as that warm water pushes fish toward the mouths, and the better fish have shown up right at the inlet drains — Port Jeff Inlet, the Mount Sinai channel edge, Northport Bay's outflow — on the last two hours of the outgoing when the current is still moving water but not screaming. Five-inch white or pearl Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the bottom in 20 to 35 feet, have taken keepers to about 5 pounds, but it's been a grind. I'd call it a two-or-three-fish trip if you put in the drift time, not a limit trip. If the water keeps warming the way it has, expect this pattern to hold or get more pronounced through the month — fluke abandoning the shallow bay water for anything with moving current and depth.

Porgies have been the reliable part of the week, which is about what you'd expect in early July. Charles Island and the reef structure around the Norwalk Islands have been giving up steady numbers on simple hi-lo rigs with clam or squid strips, bottom in 20 to 30 feet on the calmer tide stages. Nothing exciting to write home about, but a fun, dependable box-filler while you wait for the bigger tide to turn on the bass. Weakfish, on the other hand, I have nothing to report. Water's warm enough by every measure we track, and the reports just aren't there — same story as the bay systems to our south. I'm not writing that fish off for the year, but the warm-water theory alone clearly isn't the trigger people hoped it would be.

Looking ahead, the new moon spring tide peaking July 11-13 is the thing to build your week around. If the current at Stratford Shoal and Middle Ground runs as hard as I expect, I'd be there on the last two hours of the outgoing both mornings, working the rip edges with bucktails and live bunker where you can get it. The PM flood-sunset window sliding east from the Kings Point area should reach our stretch of water by the weekend — worth a sunset sit at the Norwalk Islands or off Charles Island if the bass follow the bait the way they usually do on a building spring tide. And keep an eye on the bait — if bunker and sand eels keep stacking in the narrows the way they have, and the bonito corridor to our east keeps widening the way it's been reported doing off Rhode Island, there's a real chance we see the first bonito push into the eastern Sound edge before this month is out. Too early to bank on it, but that's exactly the kind of signal worth watching for.
